idiom_name: higher-order handlers typed (req) => Promise<Response>, plus Nest guards in registration order
implementation_notes: Gates are functions with a shared type: a gate takes the next Handler and returns a Handler that verifies and then delegates, so the chain is their composition; NestJS expresses the same structure declaratively as guards implementing CanActivate, which run in registration order and each return true or false for the same request, with interceptors wrapping the handler on both sides. What replaces the classic structure: typed higher-order functions and the framework pipeline replace proxy classes; the verified principal is attached to the typed request or an AsyncLocalStorage, and the types only guarantee the shape - a field typed Principal is not evidence, so every gate still verifies for itself. The ES2015 Proxy variant is the alternative when the guarded thing is an object rather than a request pipeline.
pitfalls: A principal typed as non-optional is a compile-time promise, not a check: any cast or spread can fabricate it, so each gate must derive it from the request itself.
Declaring a guard does not register it - a controller without the decorator silently skips the gate - and Nest runs guards after middleware and before interceptors, so ordering assumptions matter.
Async context (AsyncLocalStorage) is lost across worker threads and un-awaited callbacks, silently removing the identity an inner gate was told to trust.

variants.name: Typed ES2015 Proxy handler intercepting per-operation
variants.idiom_name: ProxyHandler<T> with get/apply/set traps forwarding through Reflect
variants.implementation_notes: The language-level alternative is the ES2015 Proxy typed as ProxyHandler<Service>: a gate is a handler whose traps check authority for the intercepted operation and either forward through Reflect or throw, and gates nest by wrapping a proxy in another proxy so every access crosses each gate in turn. What replaces the classic structure: the proxy object replaces the proxy class and the trap surface replaces the hand-written method list, while TypeScript types the handler and the target precisely; the engine's invariants still hold, so traps must forward the target's own results. Use it for object-shaped services and clients, not for HTTP pipelines where the middleware chain is cheaper.
pitfalls: Private fields and this binding do not survive a proxy, and methods returned from the get trap must be bound to the target or they throw on invocation.
Traps that report non-configurable or non-writable properties inconsistently with the target make the engine throw a TypeError, so gate logic must not invent property descriptors.
Internal accesses (symbols, then, inspection hooks) pass through the trap as well, so the allow-list must be explicit or unrelated code starts breaking.
